column4: Houses God permits to be raised, فِي بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ ٱللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ, are also where His name is remembered; one ayah thus joins the section's raised building to raised remembrance.
He raises the sky and places the balance, رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ, putting the section's two opposed construction motions into one ordered creation.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations while addressing their Lord; the act gives the section's رَفَعَ its literal architectural scene and joins building to prayer.
The first House is described as وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ; this is the same House whose foundations are raised in 2:127, so placement and elevation become two states of one structure.
حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا uniquely joins the section's two terms: war “lays down” its burdens, turning relief from a load into an enacted image.
The messenger يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَٱلْأَغْلَٰلَ removes peoples' load and fetters; it closely parallels the divine removal of the addressee's burden in 94:2.
The losers carry أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ, their burdens upon their backs; this is the clearest external scene for the load that makes the back creak in the section.
The woman who نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا after making it strong supplies the section's literal thread-unravelling scene and explains how the same act images broken oaths.
لَا تَنقُضُوا۟ ٱلْأَيْمَٰنَ forbids dismantling oaths after confirming them; 16:92 then makes this abstract breach visible as untwisted yarn.
Moses prays رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى; the exact chest-opening phrase places the section's opened chest beside the prayer whose tongue-knot is loosened in 20:27.
Moses asks وَيَسِّرْ لِى أَمْرِى between opening his chest and loosening his tongue-knot, bringing ease into the same sequence of relief that the section develops.
Moses asks his Lord to loosen عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِى; unlike destructive unravelling, releasing this knot enables speech and so marks the section's positive form of undoing.
سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا states that God will make ease after hardship, the closest sequential parallel to the section's doubled assurance that ease accompanies hardship.
God wills ٱلْيُسْرَ for people and does not will ٱلْعُسْرَ; the explicit opposition clarifies the two poles compressed into the section's assurance.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ is another direct divine promise of ease to the prophetic addressee, pairing closely with the promise that follows his lifted burden.
ٱلْمَيْسِرُ وَٱلْأَنصَابُ وَٱلْأَزْلَٰمُ places gaming, erected cult-stones from ن ص ب, and lots together; it strongly recalls the source dictionary's game of a set-up peg struck by another piece.
Sacrifice عَلَى ٱلنُّصُبِ and division by arrows place an erected stone and lots in one scene, concretizing the section's secondary game-and-peg field.
The sky is asked of, كَيْفَ رُفِعَتْ, beginning the creation tableau whose mountains are erected and earth spread in 88:19–20.
The mountains are asked of, كَيْفَ نُصِبَتْ; this is the section's exact Quranic scene of massive objects set upright.
The spread earth completes 88:18–19's raised-sky and erected-mountain construction, supplying the laid-out plane beneath the elevated forms.
God رَفَعَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍۢ تَرَوْنَهَا; the heavens are a raised structure whose visible supports are absent.
Of the sky, بَنَىٰهَا explicitly says God built it; 79:28 then specifies the elevation and ordering by which that cosmic construction was made.
رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّىٰهَا raises the sky's canopy and makes it proportionate, joining elevation to structural finishing.
خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍۢ تَرَوْنَهَا repeats the unsupported-heavens image and then says mountains were cast into earth to stabilize it.
وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَضَعَهَا لِلْأَنَامِ makes the earth the corresponding thing laid down for living beings beneath the raised sky of 55:7.
وَٱلسَّمَآءَ بَنَيْنَٰهَا presents the sky as something built with power, an explicit nonlexical counterpart to the section's cluster of construction verbs.
وَٱلْأَرْضَ فَرَشْنَٰهَا lays out the earth immediately after the built sky of 51:47, reproducing the upper structure and lower plane.
The audience is asked how God بَنَيْنَٰهَا وَزَيَّنَّٰهَا and left the sky without fissures; it presents creation as an intact overhead building.
أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ ٱلْأَرْضَ مِهَٰدًا makes the earth a prepared bed, the horizontal ground for the mountain-pegs of 78:7.
وَٱلْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًا calls mountains pegs, a direct nonlexical parallel to the section's erected stake and to the mountains نُصِبَتْ in 88:19.
وَبَنَيْنَا فَوْقَكُمْ سَبْعًا شِدَادًا depicts the seven heavens above as strongly built, the stable cosmic structure opposite a back nearing structural failure.
God makes the earth a bed and ٱلسَّمَآءَ بِنَآءً, a built canopy; the paired ground and building anticipate the section's placed and raised creation forms.
God makes the earth a settled place and ٱلسَّمَآءَ بِنَآءً, then fashions human forms well; cosmic building and bodily construction meet in one ayah.
The sky is made سَقْفًا مَّحْفُوظًا, a protected roof, giving architectural force to the section's description of the heavens as raised construction.
وَنَضَعُ ٱلْمَوَٰزِينَ ٱلْقِسْطَ places just scales at resurrection, repeating the exact placement of balance in 55:7 and making placement serve measured order.
وَأَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلْوَزْنَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ commands people to set weight upright in justice; it states how the balance placed in 55:7 must be maintained.
God comes at their building مِنَ ٱلْقَوَاعِدِ and the roof falls on them; foundations raised in 2:127 here become the point from which a structure is undone.
One building is founded on reverence, while another stands on a collapsing bank and falls with its builder; the ayah turns construction and structural failure into a moral comparison.
Moses's companion straightens a wall يُرِيدُ أَن يَنقَضَّ, “wanting to collapse”; it is the most exact scene of a built thing at the instant before disassembly.
Iron blocks are raised until the gap's two sides are level and molten metal is poured over them; this is a detailed scene of erecting and consolidating a structure.
The completed barrier cannot be climbed or pierced, supplying the moment of structural firmness before its promised levelling in 18:98.
Dhu al-Qarnayn says his Lord will make the firm barrier دَكَّآءَ when the promise comes; even the tightly constructed work is ultimately dismantled by its Lord.
يُخْرِبُونَ بُيُوتَهُم بِأَيْدِيهِمْ depicts people dismantling their own houses, a direct built-object counterpart to the section's literal definition of نقض البناء.
Solomon's body remains standing on a staff until the staff is eaten and he falls; the bodily structure is held erect, then gives way when its support is removed.
The good word is a tree أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ وَفَرْعُهَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ; rooted stability and upward reach give a living analogue for a name raised on a firm base.
The bad word is a tree ٱجْتُثَّتْ مِن فَوْقِ ٱلْأَرْضِ مَا لَهَا مِن قَرَارٍ, uprooted with no stability; it reverses the section's erected and securely tied forms.
Those fighting in ordered ranks are كَأَنَّهُم بُنْيَٰنٌ مَّرْصُوصٌ, like a tightly joined building, applying structural integrity to upright human bodies.
A mountain would be خَٰشِعًا مُّتَصَدِّعًا under the Quran's descent; a received weight makes even a massive created structure crack, closely echoing the load and creaking back.
The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse to carry the trust, but the human carries it; the ayah stages a moral weight against both cosmic structures and the human bearer.
God grants Abraham and his kin لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا, a lofty true renown; this is the closest nonlexical formulation of raising a person's remembrance.
The revelation is ذِكْرٌ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ, remembrance or honor for the prophetic addressee and his people; it clarifies what an elevated dhikr can mean.
Abraham asks for لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِى ٱلْـَٔاخِرِينَ, truthful mention among later generations, furnishing the prayer-side counterpart to God raising a name.
إِلَيْهِ يَصْعَدُ ٱلْكَلِمُ ٱلطَّيِّبُ makes good speech ascend to God and says righteous work raises it; verbal remembrance acquires the upward motion of the section's construction verb.

The refuge sought from the Lord in 113:1 includes protection from ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ, blowers in knots; Lord and knots meet in one short surah, matching the source dictionary's ر ب ب knot association.
The believer grasps ٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ لَا ٱنفِصَامَ لَهَا, the firmest handhold that cannot break; it supplies the securely bound opposite of an unravelled rope.
One who turns his face to God while doing good has grasped ٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ; firm attachment is joined to the same directed stance toward the Lord as 94:8.
وَٱعْتَصِمُوا۟ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ asks the community to hold fast together to God's rope and not divide, the communal opposite of strong thread deliberately unravelled.
Those who fulfil God's covenant وَلَا يَنقُضُونَ ٱلْمِيثَٰقَ embody the positive boundary: a bond is kept from the unmaking named by the section.
Those who يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَ ٱللَّهِ مِنۢ بَعْدِ مِيثَٰقِهِ repeat the section's transfer of physical dismantling to a covenant made firm.
عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ uses the ن ص ب family for exhausting toil in the same surah that says mountains نُصِبَتْ; it exposes the fatigue/erection ambiguity surrounding فَٱنصَبْ.
People rush from graves كَأَنَّهُمْ إِلَىٰ نُصُبٍ يُوفِضُونَ, as toward an erected marker or cult-stone, giving the root's protruding object a kinetic scene.
God knows the Prophet's chest يَضِيقُ because of what people say; 15:98 answers that constriction with directed worship, paralleling opened chest followed by exertion toward the Lord.
فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ commands the chest-constricted Prophet to glorify his Lord and assume a worship posture, closely matching the section's final two imperatives.
قُمِ ٱلَّيْلَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا tells the same prophetic addressee to rise and stand at night, concretizing the devotional exertion of فَٱنصَبْ.
وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ orders the Prophet to remember his Lord's name and devote himself wholly to Him, the closest imperative parallel to turning desire toward the Lord.
قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ commands the prophetic addressee to arise for his task; 74:3 immediately directs magnification to his Lord.
وَرَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ places the Lord as the object of magnification directly after the command to rise, paralleling “stand/exert, then desire your Lord.”
وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ joins rising or standing with glorifying the Lord in a single command to the Prophet.
The Prophet is commanded to night prayer so that his Lord may raise him مَقَامًا مَّحْمُودًا; exertion culminates in an elevated, praised station.
The faithful formulation إِنَّآ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ رَٰغِبُونَ reproduces the section's directed desire toward God almost word for word.
After their garden is destroyed, its owners say إِنَّآ إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا رَٰغِبُونَ, exactly the stance toward the Lord commanded at the section's close.
The prophets call on God رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا and humble themselves; desire becomes sustained devotional action directed to Him.

God assigns Abraham مَكَانَ ٱلْبَيْتِ and orders the House purified for circumambulators and those standing, bowing, and prostrating; place, building, Lord-directed worship, and upright posture converge.
وَقُومُوا۟ لِلَّهِ قَٰنِتِينَ commands believers to stand devoutly for God, a direct bodily and devotional gloss on the section's “stand erect.”

The long night-standing command is lightened when God knows the believers cannot sustain its measure and allows فَٱقْرَءُوا۟ مَا تَيَسَّرَ; exertion, relieved load, and ease meet in one prophetic context.
The heavens nearly rupture, earth splits, and mountains collapse under a monstrous claim; speech itself places creation's built forms on the brink of structural failure.
تَكَادُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ مِن فَوْقِهِنَّ depicts the heavens nearly splitting from above, while angels glorify their Lord, joining threatened structure to the رب stance.
The ordered heavens show no تَفَٰوُتٍ and the viewer is challenged to find فُطُورٍ, any fissure; intact cosmic construction forms the boundary opposite the section's creaking, near-broken carrier.
The sky is split and becomes وَاهِيَةٌ, frail; an elevated cosmic structure reaches the state of weakness implicit in the section's cracking back.
ٱلسَّمَآءُ مُنفَطِرٌۢ بِهِ makes the sky split under the promised Day, a cosmic analogue for a structure giving way under what comes upon it.
On the Day the mountains are moved and the earth appears bare; it reverses the installed mountains and laid-out earth of the creation tableau.
God says He will scatter the mountains completely; 20:106–107 show the result as a level surface without relief, undoing the scene in which mountains are erected.
The removed mountains leave the earth قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا, a level open expanse; the protruding forms of the section's nasb image have disappeared.
لَا تَرَىٰ فِيهَا عِوَجًا وَلَآ أَمْتًا denies both hollow and rise in the level earth, explicitly marking the boundary of the erected-form image.
God says He could have raised the man by the signs, but he أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ; possible elevation is reversed by clinging to the low ground.
Believers may not تَرْفَعُوا۟ أَصْوَٰتَكُمْ فَوْقَ صَوْتِ ٱلنَّبِىِّ; human voices are forbidden to elevate themselves over the Prophet whose remembrance God raises.
إِنَّا سَنُلْقِى عَلَيْكَ قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا promises that a weighty word will be cast upon the same prophetic addressee, a precise counter-motion to the burden taken off him.
خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ describes the Event as lowering and raising; it compresses the section's downward placement and upward elevation into a reversal of rank.
Humanity is created فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ, in the best upright constitution; bodily form is presented as something set straight before the reversal in 95:5.
ثُمَّ رَدَدْنَٰهُ أَسْفَلَ سَٰفِلِينَ reverses the upright human formation of 95:4 by returning it to the lowest state, illuminating the section's elevation and lowering axis.
لَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ sets a boundary on load-bearing: another soul does not take over one's burden, whereas the section attributes relief directly to God.
The repeated rule that no bearer bears another's burden distinguishes divine removal of a burden from transferring it to a second human carrier.
Even when a heavily laden soul calls someone إِلَىٰ حِمْلِهَا, none of it is carried for them; this is the fullest boundary-scene around the section's released load.
No bearer bears another's burden, so the section's “We laid down from you” remains an act of divine relief rather than ordinary substitution.
أَلَّا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ restates the non-transferability of moral load, sharpening what is exceptional about a burden being removed.
God holds the sky أَن تَقَعَ عَلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ; the raised canopy is actively kept from falling onto the placed earth, marking the stability boundary of the construction image.
God holds the heavens and earth أَن تَزُولَا, lest they cease or slip away; maintained cosmic structure is the opposite of a form coming undone.
وَٱلسَّقْفِ ٱلْمَرْفُوعِ swears by the raised roof, naming the same overhead architectural form implied when the sky is elevated.
وَٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا بَنَىٰهَا swears by the sky and its Builder, reinforcing the section's reading of creation through building acts.
وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَمَا طَحَىٰهَا pairs the built sky of 91:5 with earth spread beneath it, another upper-structure/lower-plane scene.
After the sky is built and raised in 79:27–28, the earth is spread out; this row contributes the lower plane that completes that construction tableau.
God makes the earth بِسَاطًا, an expanse, which parallels the placed ground beneath elevated and erected forms.
God sends scripture and ٱلْمِيزَانَ so people may uphold justice; it states the human purpose of the balance placed in 55:7.
Pharaoh's wife asks رَبِّ ٱبْنِ لِى عِندَكَ بَيْتًا فِى ٱلْجَنَّةِ; a prayer to the Lord for a house to be built complements Abraham and Ishmael building while praying to their Lord.
A town lies خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا, then bones are raised and clothed with flesh; collapsed architecture and bodily reconstruction meet in the same demonstration.
The denier doubts that God will gather his bones; 75:4 answers with the ability to refashion even fingertips, treating the body as a structure reassembled.
بَلَىٰ قَٰدِرِينَ عَلَىٰ أَن نُّسَوِّىَ بَنَانَهُ specifies precise bodily reconstruction, countering the section's body at the edge of coming apart.
God خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ, creating, proportioning, and balancing the human; it supplies the body's sound construction behind the image of a strained back.
فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ says God assembled the human in the form He willed, making bodily construction explicit.
On the Hour, every pregnant female تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا; birth is literally “laying down” a carried load, an embodied secondary sense of وضع.
No female carries or تَضَعُ except with God's knowledge; the birth sense preserves the movement from bodily load to setting it down.
وَمَا تَحْمِلُ مِنْ أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ repeats carrying and laying down in pregnancy, a concrete semantic bridge between load and placement.
The term of pregnant women lasts until يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ; the legal rule rests on the same idiom of setting down one's load.
Support continues حَتَّىٰ يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ, again making childbirth an actual release of a carried burden.
Thirst, نَصَبٌ, and hunger suffered in God's path are credited as righteous action; this uses the section's nasb family in the fatigue sense of strenuous service.
Paradise's inhabitants are untouched by نَصَبٌ and never expelled, setting restful permanence against the toil sense latent in فَٱنصَبْ.
Moses says لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا; journey-fatigue supplies a clear Quranic instance of the root's non-erection sense.
In the lasting abode, لَا يَمَسُّنَا فِيهَا نَصَبٌ; absence of fatigue bounds the exertion commanded in the present life.
Job says Satan touched him بِنُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ, using the same root for affliction or exhaustion rather than an erected object.
Those who يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَ ٱللَّهِ after its binding give the covenant use of dismantling that the source derives from rope and building.
فَبِمَا نَقْضِهِم مِّيثَٰقَهُمْ names Israel's breaking of covenant as a cause of judgment, another contextual instance of the physical verb transferred to a bond.
بِمَا نَقْضِهِم مِّيثَٰقَهُمْ again treats covenant-breaking as unmaking something secured, with hardening of hearts as its consequence.
The repeatedly faithless ثُمَّ يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَهُمْ فِى كُلِّ مَرَّةٍ show a bond continually dismantled rather than held firm.
فَإِن نَّكَثُوٓا۟ أَيْمَٰنَهُم uses the related image of untying or breaking oaths; it is a nonlexical parallel to نقض a tightened covenant.
The people نَّكَثُوا۟ أَيْمَٰنَهُمْ and tried to expel the messenger, giving the oath-untying image a concrete act of betrayal.
فَمَن نَّكَثَ فَإِنَّمَا يَنكُثُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ treats breaking a pledge as untying it against oneself, close to the section's rope-derived covenant metaphor.
Misleaders carry their own burdens and some burdens of those they mislead; it extends the bodily load image from one carrier to compounded moral responsibility.
Whoever turns from the reminder يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ وِزْرًا, carrying a burden on resurrection, supplies another explicit moral load.
The misleaders will carry أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ, loads piled with further loads, intensifying the section's strained-carrier image.
The prayer asks the Lord not to lay on believers an iṣr or load beyond their capacity; it makes relief from an unbearable burden an explicit supplication.
يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ أَن يُخَفِّفَ عَنكُمْ states God's intent to lighten human beings because they were created weak, matching the direction of the removed load.
قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ establishes the Lord to whom refuge is directed; 113:4 supplies the knots that make the source's رب–knot association specific.
يَفْقَهُوا۟ قَوْلِى states the enabling result of the loosened tongue-knot in 20:27, distinguishing liberating release from destructive unravelling.
أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا۟ فِى ٱلْمِيزَانِ gives the first purpose of the balance placed in 55:7: created order must not be transgressed.
The gaming and lots of 5:90 obstruct remembrance of God and prayer; the erected-game scene therefore stands opposite the section's command to turn exertion toward the Lord.

The ayah asks about ٱلْمَيْسِرِ, a game of chance, and weighs its benefit against its great harm; it plausibly echoes the source dictionary's unusual use of “hardship” for a peg game, though it is not the same game.
God يَرْفَعِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ... دَرَجَٰتٍ uses physical elevation for honored rank, clarifying the semantic move from raising structures to raising remembrance.
God raises some messengers دَرَجَٰتٍ; prophetic distinction is expressed through the same vertical verb used for the section's elevated name.
نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَٰتٍ مَّن نَّشَآءُ converts upward constructional motion into degrees of wisdom and favor.
God raises some people فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ دَرَجَٰتٍ for a test; the ayah adds hierarchy and responsibility to the image of elevation.
نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَٰتٍ مَّن نَّشَآءُ follows Joseph's discerning stratagem, another use of elevation for granted rank rather than moved matter.
God says وَرَفَعْنَا بَعْضَهُمْ فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ دَرَجَٰتٍ in distributing livelihoods, mapping the raised/lower spatial image onto social arrangement.
God tells Jesus إِنِّى ... رَافِعُكَ إِلَىَّ, moving a person toward God rather than raising an object or a name; it marks a distinct Quranic sense of the same root.
بَل رَّفَعَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ reiterates Jesus's raising to God, a personal elevation that lies between physical lifting and bestowed honor.
وَرَفَعْنَٰهُ مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا places Idris in a high station, combining the root with explicit height.
Joseph وَرَفَعَ أَبَوَيْهِ عَلَى ٱلْعَرْشِ, physically seating his parents above on the throne; elevation becomes both spatial and honorific.
God رَفَعْنَا فَوْقَكُمُ ٱلطُّورَ, lifting the mountain over the covenant community; a massive placed object becomes suspended overhead.
The mountain is again raised over the people at covenant-taking, pairing physical elevation with a bond they are commanded to hold firmly.
God raises the mountain above them بِمِيثَٰقِهِمْ; elevated mass and covenant firmness meet in one clause.
The mountain is wrenched over them كَأَنَّهُۥ ظُلَّةٌ, like a canopy; without using رفع, it restages the raised-overhead structure during covenant-taking.
Moses asks not to be burdened مِنْ أَمْرِى عُسْرًا; hardship is pictured as something imposed on an affair, joining the section's burden and difficulty fields.
Dhu al-Qarnayn promises to speak to the righteous مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْرًا, making ease the mode of just rule.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward ease for the giver who fears and affirms the best.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ reverses 92:7 by facilitating the miser toward hardship, showing that “making easy” can lead toward a hard end.
فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ says revelation was made easy in the Prophet's tongue, linking ease, prophetic speech, and the tongue released in Moses's prayer.
فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ repeats that the revelation is eased on the prophetic tongue so people may remember.
وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِلذِّكْرِ joins ease directly to remembrance, the two gifts placed together in the section as eased hardship and raised dhikr.
The repeated refrain that the Quran is made easy for remembrance confirms that the ease–dhikr conjunction persists after the people of Noah's account.
After Thamud's account, the same refrain again couples divine facilitation with remembrance.
The fourth refrain again makes the Quran easy for remembrance, a repeated external meeting of the section's two central gifts.
ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ says God eases the human path after creation, setting facilitation within the making of the human being.
Pharaoh is called ذُو ٱلْأَوْتَادِ, possessor of stakes; the object directly recalls the source dictionary's erected wooden peg.
وَفِرْعَوْنَ ذِى ٱلْأَوْتَادِ repeats Pharaoh's association with stakes in a passage about monumental peoples, keeping the peg within an architectural-power setting.
A rope مِن مَّسَدٍ is around the woman's neck; the tightly twisted cord becomes a bodily load, bringing together rope-making and burden-bearing without the unravelling act.

The frustrated person is told to extend a rope to ٱلسَّمَآءِ and cut it; this plausibly joins a cord to an overhead support and severing, though whether “sky” means a ceiling in the scene is interpretively uncertain.

Game reached by hands and رِمَاحُكُمْ supplies a Quranic spear scene for the source dictionary's two examples—the erected spear and the spear's ṣadr as its top—but the ayah does not itself erect the spear.
